title: Solar Savings Calculator for Texas Homeowners: Real Numbers by City (2026)
excerpt: Texas has no state income tax credit for solar, but property tax exemptions and a deregulated energy market make solar a strong investment in most Texas cities. Here's how to calculate your real savings.
content:
How to Calculate Solar Savings in Texas

Calculating solar savings in Texas requires 4 inputs: your monthly electricity usage (kWh), your current electricity rate (cents per kWh), your city's peak sun hours, and your system size. The basic formula is: Annual Savings = System Size (kW) × Peak Sun Hours × 365 × Electricity Rate. For a 6kW system in Austin (5.5 sun hours, $0.124/kWh): 6 × 5.5 × 365 × $0.124 = $1,496/year in savings.

Texas Solar Savings by Major City

Solar performance varies significantly across Texas due to the state's size. Here are realistic savings estimates for a standard 6kW system after the 30% federal tax credit (net system cost approximately $12,600): Houston — $1,190/year, 10.6-year payback. San Antonio — $1,240/year, 10.2-year payback. Dallas — $1,190/year, 10.6-year payback. Austin — $1,496/year, 8.4-year payback. El Paso — $1,870/year, 6.7-year payback (best ROI in Texas). Lubbock — $1,637/year, 7.7-year payback. Midland/Odessa — $1,755/year, 7.2-year payback.

Texas Solar Incentives 2026

Texas has no state income tax (and therefore no state solar tax credit), but offers two significant incentives: First, the Texas Property Tax Code Section 11.27 exempts the added value of a solar system from your property taxes permanently. On a $15,000 system, this saves $200–$400/year in property taxes depending on your county rate. Second, many Texas utilities offer rebates — Austin Energy offers $2,500 for systems under 10kW, CPS Energy in San Antonio offers up to $1,000. Always check your specific utility's current program before getting quotes.

Texas Electricity Rates and ERCOT

Texas has a deregulated electricity market (ERCOT grid) meaning you can choose your electricity provider. Rates vary from $0.09–$0.16/kWh depending on your plan and provider. If you're on a variable rate plan (common in Texas), solar provides a natural hedge against rate spikes — Texas saw extreme rate events in February 2021 and during summer 2022. Fixed-rate plan holders benefit from solar locking in savings at their current rate regardless of future market changes.

Net Metering in Texas

Texas does not have a statewide net metering mandate. Individual utilities set their own policies. Austin Energy and CPS Energy offer solid value-of-solar tariffs. Oncor, the main distribution utility for Dallas-Fort Worth, requires retail providers to offer net metering but rates vary. If you're in a rural electric cooperative, check their specific buy-back rate before sizing your system — some co-ops offer minimal credit for exports, meaning you should size to match consumption rather than overproduce.

How to Get an Accurate Texas Solar Quote

Step 1: Pull your last 12 months of electricity bills and calculate your average monthly kWh usage. Step 2: Find your city on SolarAtlas to see your local sun hours and estimated savings. Step 3: Get quotes from 3+ installers — in Texas's competitive market, quotes for identical systems regularly vary by $3,000–$6,000. Step 4: Ask each installer for a production guarantee in writing. Step 5: Confirm your utility's net metering or buy-back rate before signing. Use the city-specific calculators on SolarAtlas to benchmark any quote you receive against real local averages.
